Question
========
Plain tabular data (rows and columns) tends to struggle with repeated information, nested details and one-to-many relationships. Why do semi-structured formats often represent this kind of data as a tree instead?

Answerlist
----------
* A tree simply looks cleaner when printed on paper.
* A tree can directly express nested details and one-to-many relationships through parent, child and sibling elements, without the extra overhead a relational database would need.
* A tree always takes up less storage space than any table, no matter what the data looks like.
* A tree can only store numbers, so it avoids the formatting issues text causes in tables.


Solution
========
Relational databases can handle one-to-many relationships too, but only by splitting the information across several linked tables, which adds organizational overhead. A tree structure avoids this by letting each element simply contain its child elements directly - for example, a university organigram can nest faculties, institutes and staff underneath each other exactly as they are related, without needing separate lookup tables.
